evidence.finding: Mean AHT increased from 375.2 seconds before the incident to 524.2 seconds afterward (+39.7%).
Mean service level declined from 86.7% to 60.4% after incident onset.
Mean ASA rose from 30.6 to 65.3 seconds (+113.3%).
Average abandonments increased from 2.2 to 13.6 per interval while answered calls declined 17.2%.
Logged-in staffing remained 49 and productive staffing was essentially unchanged, while occupancy increased from 74.4% to 96.6%.
AHT increased by approximately 40% in every queue, demonstrating a center-wide rather than localized pattern.
Account Support volume increased 16.3%, amplifying local impact, while aggregate demand declined slightly.
No platform or routing events were recorded during the full evaluation window.

primary_root_cause_detail: A synchronized center-wide increase in average handle time began at the 09:15 incident boundary. The longer workload saturated otherwise stable staffing, reduced answered throughput, increased queueing and abandonments, and drove service level below target.
recommended_actions: Identify the interaction or process change that caused the 09:15 center-wide AHT increase, including application latency, workflow changes, and contact complexity.
Activate intraday AHT alerts and capacity reforecasting when sustained AHT exceeds plan.
Use temporary overflow or cross-skilled staffing while AHT remains elevated.
Review Account Support capacity because its localized volume increase amplified service-level degradation.

rejected_hypotheses.reason: Aggregate offered volume decreased 2.6% after incident onset, and three of four queues had lower volume.
Scheduled and logged-in headcount remained constant at 49, with productive staffing changing by only -0.3%.
Queue staffing remained unchanged and all queues experienced nearly identical proportional AHT increases.
No corroborating platform event was recorded in the incident window.

stakeholder_summary: The incident was most likely caused by a sustained, center-wide AHT increase beginning at 09:15—not by higher aggregate demand or reduced staffing. Longer calls saturated available capacity, lowered throughput, and produced sustained queueing and service-level degradation.
